prompt.context: Your client, Daenerys Targaryen, is the owner of a zoo. Daenerys has always been interested in exotic animals and is interested in buying a Liger to showcase at her zoo and has hired you to help her determine what to do.
prompt.question: Should Daenerys buy a Liger for her zoo? Is the investment advisable?

clarifying_info.a: The objective is an ROI greater than 14%. ROI is defined as NPV of total profit divided by NPV of total investment.

clarifying_info.q: What products and services does the zoo offer?
clarifying_info.a: Ticket sales, merchandise sales, and shows. Most animals that you see at a zoo are already present.
No other zoos in the immediate area.
A cross between a lion and a tiger — this is a real animal.

clarifying_info.q: How many visitors does the zoo currently have?
What are merchandise and show revenues?
clarifying_info.a: Merchandise is 10% of total ticket revenue ($840k); shows are 5% of total ticket revenue ($420k). Total revenue is $9.66M.

clarifying_info.q: What are current costs and margins?
clarifying_info.a: Current costs are approximately $8.7M; current profit margin is 10%.

exhibits.title: Projected Ticket Sales and Costs if Liger is Purchased
exhibits.shows: A bar chart comparing current ticket sales (600,000 total: 300,000 adults + 300,000 children) versus projected ticket sales with the Liger exhibit (660,000 total: 330,000 adults + 330,000 children). A separate cost table lists: Maintenance $170,750 (annual), Salaries $235,150 (annual), Other Upkeep Costs $110,100 (annual); and one-time costs: Purchase of Liger $1,350,000, Transportation $675,000, Enclosure Construction $1,975,000.

framework: Internal — Incremental revenue from Liger: increased ticket sales, merchandise sales, show sales
Internal — Costs from buying Liger: purchase price, enclosure construction, food/other upkeep, trainer salaries, insurance
NPV analysis: compare PV of incremental perpetual profits against one-time investment costs; check if ROI > 14%
External — Competition: what are other zoos doing, do they have Ligers?
External — Financing: can the client afford this, will financing be needed?
External — Strategy: why a Liger vs. another animal, alternative ways to achieve the objective
External — Risks: safety risks, lifespan assumption, backlash against a genetically crossed animal

questions.prompt: Before seeing Exhibit 1, brainstorm how a Liger would impact total revenue and what costs would be associated with the purchase and upkeep.
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify three revenue lines (tickets, merchandise, shows) and distinguish one-time costs (purchase, transportation, enclosure) from recurring annual costs (maintenance, salaries, other upkeep/food/medical). Strong candidates will propose an NPV or perpetuity framework to evaluate the investment.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, perform an NPV analysis to determine whether buying the Liger is a good investment. Do NOT round numbers.
questions.guidance: Candidate must: (1) compute incremental revenue, (2) compute recurring annual costs, (3) compute annual incremental profit, (4) apply perpetuity formula (CF/discount rate) to get PV of cash flows, (5) subtract one-time investment costs to get NPV, (6) compute ROI = NPV profit / investment cost and compare to 14% target.

math.setup: Discount rate = 10%. Liger lives 100 years, so model as perpetuity. One-time costs paid at t=0; revenue begins at t=1. Perpetuity formula gives PV of cash flows one year hence.
math.answer: NPV = $500k (positive). ROI = 12.5%, which is below the 14% target but still positive and above the zoo's current 10% profit margin.

questions.prompt: What if the zoo decides to buy two Ligers — a male and a female? Would this be a good idea?
questions.guidance: Candidate should ask about procreation and incremental revenue from selling cubs. Key insight: if the pair reproduces, the cub can be sold. Guide candidate to ask about reproduction probability and cub sale price, then have them compute expected value of the cub discounted to present, add to base NPV, and compute the new ROI on total investment.

math.setup: Additional Liger costs: purchase $1.35M + transportation $675k = $2.025M. Total two-Liger investment: $4M + $2.025M = $6.025M. 90% probability of reproduction at t=0; gestation = 1 year, so cub sold at t=1 for $1M. Discount rate = 10%.
steps: Expected value of baby Liger (at t=1): 90% x $1,000k = $900k
Total NPV profit: base NPV $500k + baby Liger PV $818.1k = $1,318.1k (~$1.32M)
math.answer: ROI with two Ligers is approximately 21.88% (~20% rounded), which exceeds the 14% target. Buying two Ligers is the better investment if the client is willing to bear the added upfront cost and accepts the 10% risk of no reproduction.

brainstorming.prompt: How would having a Liger impact total revenue, and what are the potential costs associated with the purchase and upkeep?

categories.name: Revenue upside
ideas: Increased ticket sales from visitors drawn by the exotic exhibit
Higher merchandise sales tied to Liger-branded products
2-part tariff (separate admission fee to see the Ligers)
Membership/season pass sales driven by the new attraction
Renting the Ligers for events or film productions
Sale of offspring if a breeding pair is acquired

categories.name: Risks and considerations
ideas: Safety risk to staff and visitors
Life expectancy uncertainty — perpetuity assumption sensitive to lifespan
Backlash against a genetically crossed animal
Liger failing to attract incremental visitors as projected

recommendation: Buy a single Liger: NPV is positive ($500k) and ROI is 12.5%, which falls below the 14% target but is above the zoo's current 10% profit margin — the investment creates value.
Buy two Ligers (a breeding pair) if the client is comfortable with the higher upfront cost: expected ROI is ~22%, well above the 14% target, driven largely by the expected value of offspring.
risks: Life expectancy assumption — the perpetuity model is highly sensitive to how long the Liger lives; a shorter lifespan materially reduces PV
Breeding risk — 10% chance the pair does not reproduce, eliminating $818k of expected value
Incremental visitor growth may not materialize at the projected 10% level
Competitive response — other NYC-area attractions could respond and erode incremental attendance
Regulatory or public backlash against a genetically crossed hybrid animal
Safety incidents could create liability and reputational damage
next_steps: Conduct a price sensitivity analysis to determine whether ticket prices can be increased to improve ROI
Explore a 2-part tariff (separate Liger exhibit admission) to capture additional willingness-to-pay
Evaluate membership and season-pass programs that use the Liger as the anchor attraction
Consider renting the Ligers for outside events as an incremental revenue stream
Investigate why a Liger specifically — assess whether another exotic animal could achieve the same ROI with lower risk
Explore financing options to manage the upfront capital outlay
